source.title: Behind Harmful Compliance: Behavioral and Mechanistic Divergence Across LLM Jailbreaks

page_placements.theme: Runtime instructions, demonstrations and steering modulate safety

record.file_problem: No apparent problem; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests harmful fine-tuning and refusal-feature interventions using harmfulness evaluations and mechanistic repair analyses, but does not test the original studies’ first-token KL or compliant-prefill procedures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports direct harmfulness after harmful SFT, harmful RLVR, and abliteration; category-specific RLVR harmfulness; reflection-prompt effects; self-audit results; refusal-direction repair; and false-acceptance rates. No results are reported for benign fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes. Results cited from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: Harmful SFT on 64 examples is scored with a GPT judge on a 1–5 harmfulness scale on HEx-Phi and AdvBench. This closely matches the original fine-tuning attack and its measure. The study adds harmful RLVR (8–64 prompts) and rank-1 refusal-direction abliteration with directional repair, which bear on V5. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points: calibration reduces false acceptance without restoring safety or degrading capability; harmful compliance, harm recognition and capability awareness are separable; and self-audit and hallucination patterns are not robust safety signals under adaptive post-training.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares harmful SFT, judge-reward RLVR, and refusal-feature weight editing. It does not reproduce the first-token KL or compliant-prefill procedures associated with the other original source. Its principal learned comparison uses 64 AIR-Bench examples; category-specific RLVR uses 8 examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by jailbreak route and model family: reflection reduces RLVR harmfulness more than SFT; abliteration’s self-audit effects are intermediate for Qwen and near baseline for Llama; refusal-direction repair is strong for abliteration, partial for RLVR, and absent for SFT. Category-specific RLVR has a privacy exception.

fits_no_version.finding: RLVR models keep base-like self-audit ratings of harmfulness while complying. SFT collapses self-audit. Abliteration is intermediate in Qwen and near baseline in Llama.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm recognition and harmful compliance dissociate, with the degree depending on the jailbreak route.

fits_no_version.finding: A safety-reflection prompt cuts RLVR harmfulness (5.0 to 1.0 in Qwen, 5.0 to 2.7 in Llama). Effects on SFT and abliteration vary by model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time safety cues can restore refusal in parameter-jailbroken models, depending on route.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful RLVR raises false acceptance about nonexistent entities to about 0.97–0.99. Fifty calibration steps reduce it (Llama 0.02, Qwen 0.79).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful RLVR induces capability-blind compliance that is separable from harmfulness.

record.problems: The authors report no replications across training seeds and note possible sensitivity to data order, rollout sampling, and judge variability. SFT and RLVR training parameters and update counts are not fully matched. The reward is supplied by an LLM judge rather than a strictly verifiable checker. CKA, RSA, and one-dimensional refusal-direction patching are described as diagnostic and partly oracle-based; the text also does not provide numerical uncertainty estimates for the reported outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. General capability, PERSIST trait, truthfulness, ethics, and broader benchmark tables were omitted because they do not directly measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No sweep of example counts; only 64 examples (SFT/RLVR) and 8 per category (RLVR). Only two 7–8B instruct models. No LoRA or API fine-tuning.
Entirely untested; no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No count of the weights or ranks that carry safety. No pruning or low-rank isolation. Localization is tested only via a single refusal direction.
Entirely untested. Capability calibration targets false acceptance, not safety depth.

missing.what: Compliance, VHSR and Pr(V|C) for Base, SFT, abliteration, RLVR and RLVR+calibration on pooled HarmBench/BabyBLUE (e.g., Llama SFT compliance 0.460 vs base 0.233). This is a second harmfulness measure bearing on V1 and V5, not declared in rows_left_out.
Harmfulness of the privacy-trained category model and per-category on/off-category values
Harmfulness across training steps for SFT and RLVR (RLVR reaches ceiling fast; SFT trades compliance against capability)
Base-model harmfulness scores on AdvBench and HEx-Phi (about 1.0–1.6), needed as the baseline for the H and A rows
Random-direction control results for refusal patching

record.verdict_notes: The tranche was changed to T1 because the SFT arm uses harmful examples with a GPT 1–5 harmfulness judge on HEx-Phi, as in the original. Abliteration, RLVR and repair add T2/T3-style evidence. The V5 evidence concerns one refusal direction, not parameter counts. The authors describe the patching as oracle-based and diagnostic. SFT and RLVR hyperparameters are not matched, and no seed replication is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful SFT and RLVR with 64 examples, plus category-specific RLVR with 8 examples. Does not sweep example counts across the claimed range or test every harmful fine-tuning recipe.
Benign prompts are used to estimate an abliteration direction, not as ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data.
Tests a safety-reflection scaffold, not compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes that bypass safety.
Tests refusal-direction suppression and one-dimensional directional repair, but does not measure how many weights or ranks carry safety.
Does not test whether training data or objectives produce first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to deepen safety across response positions.
